extra.message: Hardcoded JWT secret key in default configuration — Attackers can forge JWT tokens and impersonate any user including administrators. [verified: Same hardcoded JWT secret 'change-me-in-production-dev-only-key' in config.py (line 7, not 6 as reported); used identically by auth.py for token signing. Duplicates Finding 0 but independently confirmed — the default is present and reachable.]

Insecure deserialization via pickle.loads on attacker-supplied data — Remote code execution on the server during pickle deserialization of attacker-crafted payload. [verified: Same pickle.loads deserialization as finding 2: attacker-controlled bytes fed to pickle.loads() at line 52.]

Server-Side Template Injection via Jinja2 user-controlled template — Remote code execution via Jinja2 template injection, full server compromise. [verified: Same Jinja2 SSTI as finding 1: user 'fragment' interpolated into Template('Result: ' + fragment).render() at line 136.]

Command injection via os.system in shell probe endpoint — Remote code execution on the application server with the privileges of the server process. [verified: Same os.system command injection as finding 0: 'host' query parameter flows unsanitized into os.system('ping -c 1 ' + host) at line 144.]

Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) via Jinja2 with user-controlled fragment — Remote code execution on the application server via Jinja2 template engine exploitation. [verified: User-supplied 'fragment' query parameter interpolated into Jinja2 Template('Result: ' + fragment).render() at line 136; SSTI payloads (e.g. __import__) achieve RCE.]

OS command injection via user-controlled host parameter in os.system call — Remote code execution on the application server with the privileges of the running process. [verified: User-controlled 'host' query parameter concatenated directly into os.system('ping -c 1 ' + host) at line 144 with zero sanitization; shell metacharacters execute arbitrary commands.]

Hardcoded database credentials in default configuration — Exposure of database credentials allowing direct database access and data exfiltration. [verified: config.py:6 hardcodes database_url default with credentials 'propertyapp:propertyapp'; database.py uses it for SQLAlchemy engine. Absent DATABASE_URL override, DB credentials are exposed in source enabling direct DB access.]

Missing brute-force protection on authentication endpoints — Attackers can brute-force user passwords without restriction, enumerate valid credentials, flood the registration endpoint with fake accounts, and abuse the password-reset endpoint. [verified: No rate-limiting middleware, SlowAPI, account-lockout, or failed-attempt tracking exists anywhere in the codebase; the login endpoint at auth.py:34 accepts unlimited credential-guessing attempts with no throttling.]

Password reset token exposed in application logs — An attacker with access to application logs (e.g., log aggregation system, developer console, CI output) can capture password reset tokens and take over arbitrary user accounts. [verified: auth.py:70 prints the full JWT reset token to stdout via print(f'...token={token}'), and the token is a real valid JWT stored in _reset_tokens and honored by password_reset_confirm; anyone with log access can take over any account.]

Unbounded file read in units CSV import enables memory exhaustion — An authenticated admin can upload a multi-gigabyte CSV file that is fully buffered into memory, causing the application to crash with OOM and denying service to all users. [verified: The import_units endpoint at imports.py:70 calls file.file.read() with no size validation. The max_upload_size (10MB) in config.py is defined but never imported or enforced anywhere in the imports router, leaving the endpoint vulnerable to unbounded memory exhaustion.]

Unbounded file read in payments CSV import enables memory exhaustion — An authenticated admin or property manager can upload a multi-gigabyte CSV file that is fully buffered into memory, causing OOM crash and denial of service. [verified: The import_payments endpoint at imports.py:103 calls file.file.read() with no size validation. Identical pattern to finding [0] — max_upload_size is dead config, no middleware or inline check limits the read, so a multi-GB upload can trigger OOM.]

Missing role restriction on maintenance ticket update enables mass assignment of sensitive fields — Unauthorized users may reassign maintenance tickets to arbitrary workers or modify ticket properties beyond their intended permissions. [verified: The PATCH endpoint uses only can_view_maintenance_ticket (a VIEW check) with no require_role() write gate, and the setattr loop at line 133 applies all MaintenanceTicketUpdate fields including assigned_to without any role-based filtering or validation, allowing any user who passes the view check to reassign tickets and manipulate sensitive fields.]

IDOR: Maintenance workers and property managers can read any message including internal admin notes by guessing message ID — A maintenance worker can enumerate message IDs and read all internal confidential communications between property admins and managers, as well as private messages between any users. A property manager can read private messages between tenants and managers of OTHER properties outside their managed scope. [verified: The get_message endpoint at /api/messages/{message_id} enforces access control (sender/recipient match, internal-note restriction) only for TENANT (lines 85-88); MAINTENANCE_WORKER and PROPERTY_MANAGER bypass all checks, letting them read any message by ID — including admin internal notes — contrary to list_messages which properly scopes both roles to their own messages or managed-property tenants]

IDOR: Property managers can view user profiles of tenants outside their managed properties — A property manager at one property can harvest PII (email, phone, full name) of all tenants and users across the entire platform, bypassing the property-scoped visibility enforced in the list_users listing endpoint. [verified: get_user checks only role (require_role), with zero property-scoping for managers — unlike list_users which explicitly calls get_managed_property_ids to scope manager visibility. No middleware, dependency, or decorator adds compensating property-level authorization; require_role checks role only, not resource ownership.]

Path traversal in vault endpoint via user-controlled ref parameter — Arbitrary file write on the server filesystem, potentially leading to code execution or data corruption. [verified: Same path traversal via 'ref' as finding 6: BASE_EXPORT_DIR / f'{ref}.json' at line 74 with no sanitization.]

Server-Side Request Forgery via user-controlled URL in relay endpoint — Access to internal network resources, cloud metadata services, or internal APIs from the server context. [verified: Same SSRF as finding 4: urlopen(endpoint) at line 110 with no URL validation.]

Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) via user-controlled URL in urllib.request.urlopen — Access to internal services, cloud metadata endpoints, and network reconnaissance from the server. [verified: urllib.request.urlopen(endpoint) at line 110 fetches a user-controlled URL with no allowlist or scheme restriction; internal services and cloud metadata endpoints are reachable.]

NoSQL injection via unsanitized user input in MongoDB query — Database compromise, data exfiltration, or arbitrary JavaScript execution on the MongoDB server. [verified: Same NoSQL injection as finding 5: user JSON passed directly as MongoDB filter in find_one(query).]

Path traversal in dock endpoint via user-controlled name parameter — Arbitrary file write on the server, potentially overwriting application code or planting web shells. [verified: Same path traversal via 'name' as finding 7: BASE_EXPORT_DIR / name with no sanitization in the dock endpoint.]

XML External Entity injection via lxml with entity resolution enabled — Arbitrary file read from the server, SSRF to internal hosts, or denial of service via entity expansion. [verified: Same XXE as finding 3: lxml XMLParser with DTD/entity resolution enabled at line 155.]

NoSQL injection via user-controlled MongoDB query filter — Unauthorized data access, query logic bypass, and potential data exfiltration from MongoDB. [verified: User-supplied JSON passed directly as MongoDB query filter via payload.get('filter', payload) into find_one(query) at line 155 area; $regex/$gt operators bypass intended query logic.]

Account enumeration via registration response — An attacker can discover which email addresses are registered in the system, enabling targeted credential-stuffing or phishing attacks. [verified: The register endpoint at auth.py:22-23 returns a distinct 'Email already registered' 400 error vs success, with no rate limiting or generic-response control to mask existence checks; the password-reset endpoint conversely uses generic messaging showing the developer knew this pattern.]

Missing Secure flag on auth session cookie — Session cookies can be transmitted over plain HTTP connections, enabling man-in-the-middle attackers on unencrypted networks to steal JWT tokens and hijack user sessions. [verified: The set_cookie at auth.py:42-48 omits secure=True while transmitting a full-session JWT token; no deployment-conditional logic or middleware adds it, so the cookie is transmissible over plain HTTP in environments without TLS termination.]

CSV formula injection in maintenance ticket export — Code execution on the victim's machine when the exported CSV is opened in spreadsheet software. [verified: MaintenanceTicketBase.title (max_length=255, no regex/validator blocking =,+, -, @) accepts formula payloads from any authenticated tenant via POST /api/maintenance; export_maintenance at exports.py:85 writes t.title unsanitized via csv.DictWriter — no prefixing or escaping exists anywhere in the chain.]

Unbounded file upload read into memory enables resource exhaustion via CSV import — Server memory exhaustion and crash from a single large file upload, causing denial of service. [verified: All three CSV import endpoints read the entire upload into memory via file.file.read().decode('utf-8') with zero size check; the max_upload_size config field exists in config.py but is never referenced anywhere in the codebase, leaving no enforced limit on a reachable authenticated path.]

CSV formula injection in payment export via unsanitized user-controlled fields — Attackers who can influence payment_method or notes fields can inject spreadsheet formulas that execute when the CSV is opened, potentially leading to command execution on the victim's machine. [verified: The /api/payments/export/csv endpoint writes p.payment_method directly into CSV cells (line 121) without sanitizing formula prefixes. payment_method is user-controllable via create/update endpoints (PaymentRecordCreate schema, max_length=50, no regex validator) and CSV import (imports.py line 117). No CSV formula sanitization utility exists anywhere in the codebase. The notes field cited in the cl]

Sensitive data (request body and auth headers) written to application logs — Authentication tokens and sensitive data exposed in log files accessible to operators or attackers who gain log access. [verified: Same sensitive-data-in-logs as finding 10: logger.warning logs Authorization header and request body at line 33.]

Open redirect via user-controlled lane parameter — Phishing attacks by redirecting users to attacker-controlled websites appearing to originate from the trusted domain. [verified: Same open redirect as finding 8: RedirectResponse(lane) at line 39 with user-controlled target.]

Sensitive data (SSN, credit card numbers) stored in plaintext on filesystem — Exposure of PII and financial data if the filesystem is compromised or backup copies are leaked. [verified: Same plaintext PII storage as finding 11: SSN and credit card data written unencrypted to JSON files at line 76.]

Sensitive PII (SSN) and financial data (credit card) stored in plaintext JSON files — Sensitive personal and financial data is stored unencrypted on the filesystem, violating compliance requirements and exposing data to anyone with filesystem access. [verified: target.write_text(json.dumps({...,'ssn':...,'card':...})) at line 76 stores SSN and credit card numbers unencrypted on the filesystem in plaintext JSON.]

Denial of service via unbounded count parameter in list generation — Server memory exhaustion and denial of service from a single request with a large count value. [verified: Same DoS as finding 12: unbounded range(count) at line 100 allows memory exhaustion.]

Unbounded resource consumption via user-controlled count parameter in list generation — Server memory exhaustion and crash, causing denial of service to all users. [verified: range(count) at line 100 has no upper bound; an attacker-controlled 'count' parameter (e.g. 10^9) causes memory exhaustion and denial of service.]

Missing security headers on all HTTP responses — Browsers will not enforce HTTPS (no HSTS), pages can be framed for clickjacking (no X-Frame-Options), and MIME-type sniffing attacks are possible (no X-Content-Type-Options). [verified: No security headers (HSTS, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, CSP, Referrer-Policy) are configured anywhere in the application; main.py registers only CORSMiddleware and no other middleware or response header logic exists anywhere in the codebase.]

Use of cryptographically broken MD5 hash algorithm — Collision attacks and hash reversal feasible, undermining integrity of any system relying on these digests. [verified: hashlib.md5() at line 77 computes MD5 digests of user input; MD5 is cryptographically broken, though no security-sensitive operation depends on the output here.]

CORS misconfiguration: wildcard origin reflection with credentials — Malicious websites can make authenticated cross-origin requests to the API using the victim's cookies, reading sensitive data. [verified: Same CORS misconfiguration as finding 9: Origin reflection with credentials=true at line 124.]

CORS misconfiguration with credential reflection from arbitrary Origin — Cross-origin data theft: malicious websites can make authenticated requests to internal endpoints and read responses. [verified: Origin header reflected into Access-Control-Allow-Origin with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials:true at line 124; ops endpoints use header-based auth so automated cookie theft is impractical, but the misconfiguration is genuine.]

Weak PRNG (random.choice) used for token/nonce generation — Predictable token/nonce values enabling replay or bypass of security mechanisms relying on these codes. [verified: random.choice() (non-cryptographic Mersenne Twister) used for nonce generation at line 151 instead of secrets module; tokens are predictable to observers.]
